item.title: The Importance of Understanding Regret
item.description:
Emotions

The Importance of Understanding Regret

A compassionate examination of regret may fuel emotional growth.

Posted July 21, 2026

Key points
  • Regret is an innate part of the human experience.
  • Self-flagellation doesn't increase psychological understanding.
  • Regret provides an opportunity to appreciate an aspect of yourself you didn't recognize before.
Source: mapo/istockphoto

As a therapist, I hear a lot about regret. “If I had only…”. “I should have known…” “How could I have…” It has always struck me as a unique emotional state — a mix of shame, blame and sadness with a sprinkle of magical thinking. On rewind and repeat, one can pop back into “before times” and imagine a different scenario with the wisdom of life lived.

In some circumstances, processing regret with others may be a useful exercise. The healing process promoted by Alcoholics Anonymous includes taking responsibility and making amends for past actions, an approach that may include some regret. Regret for egregious behavior is needed to facilitate behavioral change.

In other situations, a ruminative, private, intense regret can be a distressing psychological experience which may fuel emotional stagnation. It is unlike sorrow, a more easily shared emotion that allows the listener to join with the individual in pain and to provide compassion. If this type of fixated regret can be shared, processed and understood, it can provide the seeds for increased psychological understanding and future opportunity.

Wishful Regret

Wishful regret (my term) occurs when an individual wishes for an outcome that doesn’t have a bearing in reality. A journalist who received a D in college freshman chemistry exclaims, “If I had just become a doctor, I wouldn’t have to worry about finances now!”

This regret avoids a deeper discussion. Did the individual ever have an interest in science? Did his parents expect him to pursue medicine? How has it felt to pursue a passion that has less stability but more personal meaning? What would it have been like to sacrifice years of life to an intensive scientific pursuit that didn’t sync with their cognitive strengths?

Wishful regret is a shortcut that may cut off a more complex discussion of present worries and concerns.

Regret as a Simplification

Regret may take a simplified view of a past situation, hiding a more complex discussion of the individual’s current needs:

A marketing analyst in her late 30s with two little children reads travel magazines for fun, and feels a deep regret that she didn’t travel more during her 20s when she had more freedom.

She imagines what it would be like to see the fjords in Norway, or ride a camel in Morocco. She chastises herself for missing the opportunity to explore the world when she had the chance.

In this case, the regret may be hiding two more complex experiences.

In the haze of early childhood parenting, the mother may be disconnected from the details of her twenties. She has forgotten that she didn’t have funds or extensive time off to travel during this decade. She is overlooking that her younger self’s investment in work and community led her to her current loving partner and interesting and challenging job.

article continues after advertisement

It might be more helpful to understand the wish to travel as a mother’s wish for more autonomy. Parents of young children have lost a significant amount of personal time for themselves. Independence that was available before children now requires foresight and planning.

The fixation on inaccessible, expensive, exotic travel may lessen if the mother prioritizes her own needs a bit more within the family system. Maybe she can’t go to Thailand, but can she arrange a babysitter so she and her spouse can have a child-free dinner at the new local Thai restaurant? Maybe she can’t go hiking in the Alps, but could she look for an opportunity to take a walk with a friend without the children?

A deeper discussion of her regret may lead to a greater understanding of the past and her current emotional needs.

Deep-Seated Regret

Major regret for a pivotal past decision can cause substantial distress.

She cheated on me when we were dating, and I just learned she has had a year-long affair—why did I marry her in the first place?

Why did I ignore the fact I was losing weight and avoid the doctor over the last several months? Now I’m undergoing a work-up to rule out a malignancy.

There is formidable emotional pain associated with these expressions of regret. What is the way forward?

At first, the regret may serve as a way to assert control in response to a chaotic scenario. Forced to face upsetting news, the knee-jerk reaction is to return to a prior time in one’s head to create an alternate ending. Repeating “How could I have…” is easier than facing the intense feelings bubbling underneath: fear, upset, and grief at the unfairness of it all.

If the individual plants themselves in the regret loop, it adds self-flagellation to an already painful experience. Instead, amongst the understandable pain, there is an opportunity to learn something important about oneself. Looking backwards, psychotherapy may uncover some buried emotional truths. What would it have felt like to end the relationship with numerous red flags? There was a reason the younger self moved forward toward marriage despite the concerns. To create a better future, there needs to be a deeper psychological understanding of this prior moment and what drove the decision-making.

article continues after advertisement

For the patient who ignored concerning physical symptoms, what would it have been like to prioritize self-care? What obstacles were in the way, precluding increased attention to one’s own needs? If high anxiety around doctor visits prevented appropriate follow-up, it would be helpful to address the anxiety through therapy or medications, especially if a more intensive treatment course will now be necessary.

In our life journey, we can’t see around the corner to see what is coming next. Regret is part of being human. Insight is only available looking backwards. If regret occurs, it means, for any number of reasons, you didn’t appreciate something important at that time. A compassionate excavation of your decision-making creates a learning opportunity.

item.title: Courage Is the Pivot Point Where Everything Changes
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

Courage Is the Pivot Point Where Everything Changes

A Personal Perspective: How would more courage change your life?

Posted July 21, 2026

Courage is the Pivot Point Where Everything Changes
Source: Anastasia Lashkevich / Pexels

This is part one of a two-part series.

The Greek poet Virgil said, "Fortune favors the bold." I first discovered this truism as an older teenager, and it has served me well through the years.

As a high school student, I wanted to be involved in student government. Each year I ran for class office, but each time I took the more timid route and ran for one of the lesser offices, never class president. I ran for VP, or treasurer, or secretary, and I was never elected. My last chance came at the end of eleventh grade as a rising senior. This time I threw caution to the wind and ran for the biggest prize: Student Council President. And I won. It was a game changer for me.

Overnight, I became one of the most popular kids in school. The office came with tons of responsibilities, all of which served to build my confidence. I started asking some of the prettiest girls on dates. Many of them said, “No,” but I was proud of myself for even asking — something I would’ve never done just a year earlier. The important factor was recognizing that being bold was what opened the doors of opportunity for me. I was determined to keep being bold, and as a result, more good things came my way.

Years later, when I became a motivational speaker, I encouraged people to be bold. I would ask, “How would your life be different if you were ten times bolder?”

As a speaker on creativity and innovation, I changed from encouraging people to be bold to taking risks. A willingness to take risks is a big part of innovation, and becoming comfortable with risk is a key characteristic of creative people.

I speak to elementary school students and encourage the kids to push their fear aside and stand up for themselves. To help them, I teach two techniques that enable them to peacefully de-escalate bully attacks.

Remarkably, I never equated “being bold,” “taking risks,” and “standing up for yourself” as being aspects of courage. I didn't learn how important courage is until just a few years ago when I started studying states of consciousness. My interest in states of consciousness came when I realized from personal experience that they can affect our health.

Your State of Consciousness Is How You Feel About Yourself and Your Outlook on the World

I'd heard many times that if I raised my state of consciousness, I would be more successful. But I didn't really understand the concept.

It wasn't until I went through the grief of a heartbreak that I recognized it. My state of consciousness was so low that I got sick, then sicker, and finally sickest: landing me in the hospital. I'm normally a healthy person, but after I went through three successive yet separate and different illnesses that were each worse than the last, I fully understood it was my low state of consciousness that was making me sick.

article continues after advertisement

I was finally beginning to understand it, but still... I had no clue how to raise my state of consciousness.

It would be another three years until I would begin to learn that. A friend recommended a book to me titled Power Vs. Force by psychiatrist David Hawkins, MD, PhD. The book provided me with a scale of the various levels of states of consciousness. Those are from lowest to highest as follows: shame, guilt, apathy, grief, fear, desire, anger, pride, courage, neutrality, willingness, acceptance, reason, love, joy, peace, and enlightenment.

Each level up to pride are negative states of consciousness. The first level that is a positive state of consciousness is courage.

Here’s How I Went Through Several Levels in One Year

I was severely bullied as a kid in elementary school in first through third grade. I was bullied by older boys. I was bullied by the kids at school because I was bullied — abused if you will — by my parents. My mother was a narcissistic perfectionist who was obsessed with appearances; my father was her enforcer. I was beaten, shamed, and criticized frequently.

My sense of self-esteem, and state of consciousness, were so low I walked around with my head down and my shoulders hunched over, which is a survival posture people use be invisible and symbolically protect their heart...

...to be continued in part two.

item.title: When OCD Builds on Trauma
item.description:
OCD

When OCD Builds on Trauma

The neuroscience behind why trauma makes OCD feel so convincing.

Posted July 21, 2026

Key points
  • Trauma sensitizes the brain's threat detection system, making intrusive thoughts feel more real.
  • Trauma weakens inhibitory learning, making it harder to learn that you are safe in the present moment.
  • OCD and a history of trauma impact the brain's ability to regulate emotions.
  • Trauma can shape what OCD latches onto, making obsessions feel more believable and compulsions feel needed.

When compulsions feel protective because your brain is screaming at you that you're in danger, it makes it very challenging to engage in obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) treatment. Your brain can pull from traumatic experiences, creating a very convincing story that these compulsions are necessary because they feel like they are the only path to safety and certainty.

While OCD and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) or complex post-traumatic stress disorder (C-PTSD) are distinct conditions with different underlying mechanisms, they frequently overlap. In fact, emerging research suggests that individuals with features of C-PTSD often experience greater OCD symptom severity than those with OCD alone (D'Angelo et al., 2024).

This does not mean trauma causes OCD. Many people experience trauma and never develop OCD, while many individuals with OCD have no significant trauma history. Like most psychological disorders, OCD develops through a combination of genetics, neurobiology, learning experiences, and environmental factors.

What trauma can do is influence how OCD is experienced. It can make intrusive thoughts feel more believable, more emotionally charged, and more difficult to disengage from. Understanding the neurobiology behind why this happens can reduce shame and help explain why treatment may feel particularly challenging. It is also important for clinicians to understand the overlap to determine the need for trauma interventions. Here are five ways OCD builds on trauma based on neurobiology.

1. Trauma sensitizes the brain's threat detection system.

One of the most replicated findings in trauma research is increased activation of the amygdala, the brain region responsible for detecting potential threat, our "fight or flight" system (Shin & Liberzon, 2010; Pitman et al., 2012). From a survival perspective, this makes perfect sense: If someone has lived through repeated danger, the brain becomes increasingly efficient at recognizing anything that might signal harm. This adaptation is extremely protective and helpful when we are in traumatic situations, especially for folks who have experienced multiple traumatic events throughout their life.

The challenge is that the amygdala is designed to detect possible danger, not to determine whether danger is actually present. For someone living with OCD, intrusive thoughts already trigger the brain's alarm system. When trauma heightens our brain's threat detection, those same thoughts may feel even more urgent and worthy of attention. The thought isn't simply uncomfortable; it feels life-threatening.

2. Fear learning becomes stronger and harder to update.

Trauma also changes how the brain learns from threatening experiences. Fear conditioning teaches us what to avoid to stay safe. Again, this makes a lot of sense from a survival standpoint. Updating that response relies on inhibitory learning: building a new, competing "safety" memory strong enough to override the original fear, rather than erasing it (Craske et al., 2014).

Trauma appears to directly disrupt this process. Research using fear-potentiated startle shows that people with PTSD have measurable difficulty suppressing fear even when a clear safety signal is present. This finding was consistent enough that it's been proposed as a physiological marker of PTSD (Jovanovic et al., 2010).

article continues after advertisement

This matters for OCD treatment because exposure and response prevention (ERP) relies on the same mechanism: each time someone tolerates discomfort without performing a compulsion, the brain forms a competing "safe" association that gradually inhibits the original threat prediction. When trauma has both strengthened the original fear and weakened the brain's ability to realize it's safe, ERP can initially feel much harder because the nervous system's "off switch" takes longer to engage.

3. The alarm system can overpower the thinking brain.

Healthy emotion regulation depends on communication between the amygdala and the prefrontal cortex, which helps us evaluate evidence, regulate emotional responses, and recognize when an alarm may be false. Trauma research consistently demonstrates decreased regulation from the prefrontal cortex during threat processing (Shin & Liberzon, 2010). At the same time, neuroimaging studies of OCD consistently implicate dysfunction within cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuits involved in error detection, habit formation, and cognitive control (Gillan et al., 2016).

Together, these processes can make it incredibly difficult to simply "ignore the thought." This isn't a lack of willpower or use of skills in the client; it's the brain prioritizing protection.

4. Trauma increases the meaning attached to intrusive thoughts.

Not all intrusive thoughts carry the same emotional weight. One reason trauma-related OCD often feels especially convincing is that the obsessions are frequently connected to themes that already carry emotional significance. Research has begun demonstrating that trauma can shape the content of OCD symptoms (Wadsworth et al., 2023):

  • Someone who experienced abuse may become consumed by fears of harming others or being harmed.
  • Someone who has experienced childhood trauma may have obsessions about harm coming to their own children.
  • Someone with medical trauma may develop health-related obsessions.
  • Someone who has experienced interpersonal betrayal may become trapped in obsessive doubts about a new relationship.

The trauma can impact what OCD latches onto. When a thought connects to something that genuinely happened, it naturally feels more believable.

5. Compulsions can feel like protection.

Perhaps the most important concept to understand is that compulsions often feel protective. All of the checking, researching, reviewing conversations, monitoring emotions, or seeking reassurance can feel necessary. These behaviors may temporarily reduce emotional discomfort, but they also reinforce the belief that these compulsions are needed in order to feel safe.

article continues after advertisement

For individuals with trauma histories, this can become even more complicated. If vigilance once helped someone navigate an unsafe environment, or if it feels necessary to prevent a traumatic event from occurring again, letting go of compulsions may feel like abandoning the very strategy that keeps them safe. This doesn't mean compulsions are protective today; it means they once made sense. Understanding this distinction allows treatment to be approached with compassion rather than self-criticism.

Recovery Is About Updating the Brain, Not Erasing the Past

One of the most hopeful findings from neuroscience is that the brain remains capable of change throughout life. Trauma may shape how your brain responds to fear, but it doesn't determine what's possible in treatment. OCD, even alongside trauma, is highly treatable through evidence-based approaches like exposure and response prevention (ERP), Acceptance & Commitment Therapy (ACT), or inference-based cognitive behavioral therapy (I-CBT).

If you're living with both, the goal isn't to erase what happened to you; it's to help your brain learn that the survival strategies it built aren't needed in every situation anymore. You may wonder whether you need to get treated for your OCD or trauma first. The honest answer is: It depends on you. Research suggests it comes down to how your OCD and trauma symptoms are connected (Pinciotti et al., 2022). If they operate somewhat independently, working on one first often helps. However, if they're tangled together (e.g., compulsive checking driven by fear of being hurt again), addressing both at the same time tends to be more effective.

There's no universal rule here, and that's actually good news: It means treatment can be shaped around how these two parts of your experience show up for you, not forced into a one-size-fits-all order. I recommend exploring trauma treatments such as cognitive processing therapy (CPT), prolonged exposure (PE), eye movement desensitization and reprocessing therapy (EMDR), or Internal Family Systems (IFS) to see which resonates with you. I also recommend finding a therapist who specializes in both OCD and trauma, because recognizing the nuance between the two is important.

article continues after advertisement

Remember, healing is not about trying to erase the past; it's about creating a new relationship with your past and reprocessing it safely. If parts of OCD treatment have felt slow or harder than you expected, that's not a sign you're failing. It's a sign that your brain is doing its job of protecting you and is now learning something new. Freedom is possible; you just have to keep going.

To find a therapist, please visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: Is “We the People” Still Possible?
item.description:
Psychology

Is “We the People” Still Possible?

There’s a surprising reason for hope that we can overcome “us versus them.”

Posted July 21, 2026

Key points
  • Belonging can unite people, but it can also be misused to exclude others.
  • Group boundaries can change, allowing people to build a wider sense of “we.”
  • Stronger communities require shared spaces, trust, and institutions that foster belonging.

This month, as the United States celebrated its 250th anniversary, the immortal phrase “we the people” appeared on parade banners, in commemorative essays, in speeches, and across celebrations. The phrase evokes the possibility that people across a diverse society can hold a meaningful identity in common. Even beyond the United States, in countries around the world, “we the people” is shorthand for the idea of the shared public good.

Still, at a time of deep polarization and political gridlock, those three words that form the opening of the preamble of the Constitution can feel more and more elusive as an everyday reality.

Looking at the state of societies globally, it’s now an open question:

Is “we the people” still possible?

Or are we more realistically consigned to a world of “us versus them”?

It’s easy to conclude that “us versus them” is one of the oldest features of human nature. We are group-forming beings. We sort, compare, and defend our own. This is part of how people have survived, organized, and defended themselves across history. The fact is that it’s easier to organize people when there’s an “other.”

Consider the challenge of climate mobilization. For a time, many climate campaigners tried to frame the climate crisis as requiring a “World War II–style mobilization.” The point was understandable—climate change is an existential threat that demands shared sacrifice, public investment, technological transformation, and a willingness to act beyond short-term self-interest.

Yet the analogy exposed something about group psychology. World War II mobilization was sustained by a literal human enemy. There was an opposing force people could name, see, fear, and fight. Climate change doesn’t present itself in the same way. It’s a systematic challenge where there’s no single villain whose defeat would solve the problem.

The psychology of “us versus them” can generate intensity, sacrifice, and solidarity in ways that appeals to the common good often struggle to match.

Social psychology confirms this. In Henri Tajfel’s “minimal group” experiments, people showed favouritism toward members of their own group even when the groups were assigned on trivial or arbitrary grounds. People don’t need much reason to form an “us.” And once there is an “us,” a “them” can quickly emerge, because group identity often gains strength through contrast.

The same longing for belonging that brings people into community can also be redirected into exclusion, fanaticism, and violence. When people feel unseen, humiliated, displaced, or powerless, a demagogue can offer a counterfeit form of belonging by giving them someone to blame.

I have come to think of this as the shadow side of belonging.

article continues after advertisement

It looks like connection, and it may even feel like connection at first. It can offer a shared language, a shared enemy, and a shared sense of purpose. Yet this kind of belonging is hollow because it builds cohesion for some by denying dignity or respect to others. It offers people the feeling of being part of something larger, but only by narrowing the circle of moral concern.

Yet this isn’t the whole story of human nature.

Many of the problems that most require collective action—including climate, but also AI, inequality, loneliness, and democratic distrust—don’t come with a simple enemy. They require a broader and more mature form of belonging. They require something bigger than unity against an adversary. They require commitment to a shared future.

And, thankfully, human beings also raise children together, mourn together, build institutions for public service, and make sacrifices for people we will never meet. Beyond tribalism, we are also wired for care, collaboration, mutual aid, and compassion.

The key psychological question is which identity becomes most salient. Are we primarily insiders and outsiders, winners and losers? Or can we also remember that we are neighbours, citizens, parents, workers, caregivers, and members of one human family?

Here’s the biggest reason for hope: Group boundaries are never fixed. They can narrow, but they can also widen. Under the right conditions, people can come to see former strangers as part of a larger “we.”

So how do we promote an ethos of “we the people” that’s grounded in genuine belonging?

First, we need to get beyond online sorting systems that profit from sorting people into opposing camps. Personalized feeds can expose us to different villains, different facts, and different moral realities. We need to create more shared attention in everyday life, through meeting places and shared practices like libraries, community meals, service projects, neighbourhood walks, sports leagues, rituals, and public spaces where people encounter one another as real human beings.

article continues after advertisement

Second, we need to solve real problems together. People build trust when they work side by side cleaning up a park, rebuilding after a flood, mentoring young people, caring for elders, serving meals, planting trees, or deliberating over a local budget.

Third, we need to practice a psychology of the wider “we.” This is the perennial moral calling to put ourselves in another person’s shoes. It can begin with intellectual humility, like admitting, “I might be wrong.” It can mean asking, “What fear, wound, loyalty, or need might be underneath the troubling behaviour that I see?” It’s the ethic of seeking to understand. Understanding is not the same as condoning. It is the beginning of responding to the conditions that allow destructive forms of belonging to take hold.

Overall, we need to build belonging into the institutions that shape our lives. Schools, workplaces, media platforms, faith communities, governments, and businesses all help determine whether people feel respected, rooted, heard, and able to exercise agency. Belonging cannot depend solely on individual goodwill; it must also be supported by the systems through which we live together.

“We the people” has never been complete—in virtually any society I know of.

But the fact that “we the people” has been incomplete doesn’t mean it’s impossible. It means it’s a practice, a discipline, and a moral and psychological vision that we have to work to make real.

item.title: The Cult of Jung
item.description:
Therapy

The Cult of Jung

The insular circle Carl Jung built, and its path through self-help today.

Posted July 21, 2026

Key points
  • Jung originated several prevailing ideas in psychology, organized around his own authority and charisma.
  • Clinical popularity and wide acceptance does not protect a training institute from authoritarian patterns.
  • A quota limiting Jewish membership was enforced by the Jungians, with written materials being quasi-religious.

Carl Jung gave us the shadow self and asked us to consider who we are within a system of classification. His ideas traveled far beyond the psychoanalysis room, cascading through the mythology of the wildly popular Myers-Briggs personality test and decades of self-help writing. Two things remain true: one, that his clinical ideas genuinely helped patients, and two, the circle around him also organized itself around one man's personal authority.

While the early Jungian world was nothing like Scientology or NXIVM, the structure of the early Jungians falls well within the bounds of a cult-like atmosphere, complete with its own charismatic figurehead.

Applying the BITE Model

The BITE Model, which I developed, examines four kinds of influence a group exerts over its members, and the letters stand for Behavior, Information, Thought, and Emotional control.

Behavior control governs what you do, information control governs what you're allowed to know, thought control shapes how you interpret the world, and emotional control manages how you're permitted to feel.

I also describe an "Influence Continuum," a sliding scale running from healthy and constructive on one end to authoritarian and destructive on the other.

Information within the early Jungian environment flowed on two tiers, one for insiders and one for everyone else. Jung's Red Book, the private record of the hidden foundation of his psychology, was not published until 2009, nearly a century after he wrote it. For decades, the movement's most important texts circulated only among trusted insiders.

The Analytical Psychology Club of Zurich also maintained a written cap on Jewish membership, which was limited to 10 percent of members and 25 percent of guests at lectures.

The Club's own Executive Committee acknowledged this history decades later in a 1993 memorandum. Initially, the Club claimed the document was a secret of the Executive Committee unknown to ordinary members. This claim was later proven inaccurate after older members confirmed the unwritten understanding had been known and discussed long before.

Critics have argued Jung's writings on Jewish psychology, including his writings that state, “the Aryan unconscious has a higher potential than the Jewish,” cannot be separated from the broader pattern of his thought, and his actions in the 1930s.

The historian Sonu Shamdasani has disputed the "cult" framing, yet other analysis pulls the opposite way. For example, Carrie Dohe's independent 2016 research showed that Jung had framed the German national experience as a collective confrontation with inner divinity, arguably presenting his views as religious.

article continues after advertisement

In general, I find Jungian language functions as a closed, self-sealing system, and by that, I mean that once you adopt it, almost any experience can be reinterpreted through its vocabulary of archetypes and complexes.

In this context, an "archetype," in Jung's usage, is a universal symbolic pattern, and a "complex" is an emotionally charged cluster of memories. Once a person adopts the framework, virtually every experience can be reinterpreted through Jung's archetypes, complexes, persona, anima, animus, and shadow material.

This is a feature of all interpretive systems to some degree, but in the early Jungian inner circle, disagreement with Jung's interpretations was often pathologized, meaning they were to be taken as evidence of mental illness or resistance to getting better.

Is Jungian Analysis a Cult?

It would be a mistake to throw the baby out with the bathwater and discard what works, as there is some evidence that incorporating Jungian depth therapy holds value. However, the initial structure the Jungians built does arguably display cult-like features such as its black-and-white perspective on what therapy should be, and how resistance to its structure constitutes resistance to recovery. His writings on Jewish citizens and their psyches did not dwell in a silo, but instead, were distributed and interpreted by early Jungian analysts despite their insistence to the contrary.

The reason I dwell on it is that the same temptation is alive today. We should be careful that we are not simply appealing to the charismatic psychotherapy preachers of our own moment, or basing our practice on faith that an idea works because a compelling figure insists it does.

We must be willing to question the current narratives, and be willing to set aside a modality that isn't helping our patients, no matter how beloved or well-branded it is. Above all, we must always respect the patient's freedom to walk away without being pathologized for it.

item.title: The Problem With Pushing Resilience
item.description:
Adolescence

The Problem With Pushing Resilience

Personal Perspective: We need to stop telling the “snowflakes” to toughen up.

Posted July 21, 2026

Should the “snowflake generation” just be more resilient?
Source: AI generated free download by Ridderhof at Pixabay

I have a problem with resilience. Or rather, a problem with the [mostly] Gen X notion that Gen Z need more of it. Being an adolescent or young adult is tough, and tougher now than it was for Generation X when we were experiencing our own adolescence and young adulthood. Modern life is furnished with social and political inequity, extreme weather events, widespread poverty, pandemics, racism, homophobia and transphobia, violence against women and girls, exploitative porn, misogynistic media, non-consensual image-sharing, cyberbullying and war. This state of so-called “permacrisis” affects us all, to a greater or lesser extent, but it impacts Gen Z more than older adults because these events have been prevalent for a greater portion of their lives than they have been for ours.1

Another thing that makes modern life hard for Gen Z is the amount of choice on offer. They are sold the myth that this is a good thing, but that’s not true. Making choices is hard, because it results in change, which is tough in and of itself. Making a choice also means giving something up, which leads many to experience short-term fear of missing out (FOMO) and sometimes long-term regret. The more choices we have, the more we must turn down, and the more likely we are to experience overwhelm, FOMO and regret.

This was demonstrated in a well-known psychological study using jam.2 Psychologists set up a tasting booth in a supermarket that displayed either six flavours of jam or 24. When shoppers visiting the tasting booth were offered a choice of six jams, almost 30% bought a jar. Of those offered 24 varieties, only 3% made a purchase, suggesting that too much choice hampered their motivation to buy. In short, too much choice leaves people feeling stuck and unmotivated.

Thanks to the internet, Gen Z are exposed to infinite options in all areas of life: what to wear, what to watch, what to eat, who to date and what to do with their lives. Many are experiencing a kind of decision fatigue which feels debilitating to the extent that even the simplest of choices are beyond reach and leave them feeling stuck.

To add insult to injury, while experiencing debilitating stuck-ness within the context of permacrisis, Gen Z is told that these are "the best years of their lives”. Some of them play into this fallacy, by broadcasting their painstakingly curated lives in filtered squares online, accompanied by the hashtag #livingmybestlife. The truth—in real life (IRL)—is that many are living their worst life, just like all other Gen Z-ers pretending they’re not. Having the “these are the best years of your life” myth debunked should come as a relief; imagine how miserable it would be if our best lives were already behind us by the time we reached 30? Being young is hard, for all the reasons I’ve mentioned, not to mention the hotbed of hormones making everything seem like a matter of life and death. And sometimes it literally is a matter of life and death: Remember COVID-19?

article continues after advertisement

The accumulated stuff of modern life can feel overwhelming and is often what brings Gen Z to therapy, often at a point of personal crisis and sometimes as a last resort after they’ve already tried to be more resilient. Surviving modern life is not about getting the delicate “snowflake” generation to toughen up. Resilience is not something that can or should be indoctrinated into them so that they can withstand whatever sh*t life throws at them. Surely it would be better to do something to stop the sh*t landing than to try to change the generation on whom it lands heaviest? Which is why I engage troubled, confused, overwhelmed and stuck young people in therapeutic relationships, and think with them about their lived realities, rather than tell them to put up and shut up, and just be more resilient.

item.title: Easing Household Tension Around Money After Divorce
item.description:
Divorce

Easing Household Tension Around Money After Divorce

Tips for handling money conversations with your children.

Posted July 21, 2026

Key points
  • Talk about money honestly with kids using age-appropriate language and examples.
  • Set clear expectations at home about spending changes and adjustments.
  • Involve children in budgeting and household tasks to create stability.
Source: Katie Harp / Unsplash

One of the most common emotions divorced parents experience, especially the spouse who was the lower- or non-earning spouse during the marriage, is tension around money. Whether there’s not enough of it or a parent believes they’ve been treated unfairly financially, it can change both the tone and the operation of the household.

Kids are perceptive and pick up on these kinds of changes easily. As a parent, it’s up to you to shield them from conflict while ensuring they live in reality. Though I’m a family law attorney, I was also once a newly divorced mom of four school-aged kids (now grown) who faced similar challenges. These are my tips for easing household tension around money after divorce.

Discuss Money in Honest, Age-Appropriate Ways

When kids come to you and ask if they can have their birthday party at the skating rink this year instead of in the backyard, or ask if you can buy them the latest (and very expensive) designer sweatshirt you know will be out of style in a few months, and it’s not in your budget, say so. But in a gentle way, one that’s appropriate for the child’s age.

This is not the time or place to talk about how this is all their other parent’s fault, or that their other parent should pay for it, even if you believe this to be true. Those kinds of comments can only cause the child to resent the other parent, not to mention resent you, which inevitably reflects back on the child and makes them feel bad for a whole host of reasons.

The same goes for admonishing the child for asking, even if you think they should understand your family’s financial picture. Understanding is not the same as acceptance, and it’s up to you to reframe what they are perceiving as negative as something positive. That begins with setting or reinforcing clear expectations about what’s going on in the household.

Set Clear Expectations About Financial Changes at Home Post-Divorce

How well you frame your post-divorce financial circumstances will go a long way toward setting a positive tone in your home, even as you cut back on spending in certain areas. Call it a period of adjustment. Refer to it as temporary. Let your children know that circumstances can improve, and that budgeting and saving up for the extras can make them more meaningful.

Additionally, invite your children to get creative, perhaps by coming up with the weekly grocery list and recipes that make use of the items you already have at home, or by reimagining pantry staples. Have everyone pitch in with cleaning so you can reallocate the money for a house cleaner to something else far more necessary or enjoyable, perhaps a family outing or vacation. Budgeting, saving, and enjoying the fruits of it, including the sense of stability taking control of your situation brings, can be fun for the entire family as well as benefit everyone in it.

Create a Sense of Stability Even When Finances Have Changed

While inviting children to get involved is helpful in stabilizing what divorce may have destabilized, a sense of safety will ultimately come from the top—you. No matter how much you scrimp and save, how hard you work, or how much you plan, you may still find yourself feeling insecure, bad about yourself, and angry, given your current circumstances.

article continues after advertisement

This is understandable, and if your kids see you this way or ask why you’re not having a good day, explain to them that you’re human, that everyone has difficult moments, and that the goal should be to honor those emotions as you move through them. In this way, you’re modeling emotional regulation and coping skills for your children.

Though you want to limit them from seeing you at your most vulnerable, it won’t always be possible. That’s OK. Seeing you this way lets your kids know that feeling a range of emotions is natural and that they can express how they’re feeling, too, without always having to put on a strong face.

Keep Children Out of Adult Financial Conflict

Because kids are so astute, including young children, they will know if you and their other parent are fighting, even if you don’t do it in front of them. They may overhear you talking about an argument with someone else or simply pick up on your mood after communicating with your ex. As much as you can, keep your children out of adult conflict.

Should it happen in front of them, do your best to diffuse the situation peacefully and table the conversation for another time. Your children learn conflict resolution skills from you. And if you demonstrate that you are incapable of having a conversation without screaming, calling someone names, or engaging in histrionics, or, on the other hand, are willing to allow someone to berate you and otherwise treat you badly, your children will learn that, too.

So, ask yourself how you would want your children to react if their children were watching. What would you tell them to do? Whatever your answer would be, tell yourself the same thing. And remember, though money might be getting you down and be something you can’t completely control (at least not yet), your relationship with money and how you manage your emotions around it is.

item.title: Why the Lizard Brain Model and Other Science Myths Persist
item.description:
Neuroscience

Why the Lizard Brain Model and Other Science Myths Persist

The norms of the social world of research may impede our access to information.

Posted July 21, 2026

Key points
  • In the medical field, it may take an average of 17 years for research findings to get to clinicians.
  • For the disconfirmed triune "lizard" brain model, the lag is at nearly three decades.
  • As a result, many popular trauma-healing modalities are built on a foundation of the triune brain.
  • There are ways to update our knowledge and step away from disconfirmed models.
Source: Daniel Frank / Pexels

This post is Part 2 of a series.

In part 1 of this article, we explored some of the reasons for the research lag that exists between what researchers know and what clinicians and the general public may think is true.

This lag can be astonishingly lengthy (in the medical field, researchers found that it may take an average of 17 years for research findings to make their way to clinicians).

A similar lag exists in neurology and psychology, which means that much of what we think we know may have been disconfirmed decades ago.

We explored the famous—and mistaken—triune brain model that neuroscientist Paul MacLean began developing nearly 80 years ago. This model assumed that we had an unevolved lizard brain in charge of our impulses, and a slightly more evolved mammalian brain in charge of our emotions. This model also claimed that we could use our allegedly more evolved human brain to control our lizard-ish and mammalian tendencies.

This model separated humans from "mere" animals and impulses, and it helped us (incorrectly) see emotions as lower than and separate from logic. And sadly, it taught us to attempt to control, suppress, or extinguish our emotions (and glorify logic and rationality) instead of learning how and why emotions work.

It was an interesting idea, but it was found to be wrong, and most neuroscientists moved on to more grounded ideas way back in the 1990s.

However, due to the research lag, this disconfirming information was not available to clinicians or the general public for many decades.

How the lizard brain myth grew

Many college-level textbooks—and specifically, many Psychology 101 textbooks—referred to the triune brain as a real model until at least 2017.

That's a research lag of more than a quarter-century, and as a result, many therapists, counselors, and psychologists were taught an incorrect model of the brain and emotions—as if it were still valid—many years after the model had been disconfirmed.

article continues after advertisement

This research lag has meant that clinicians are still using the triune model today to explain emotions, human behavior, and the assumed aftereffects of trauma.

In fact, many popular trauma-healing modalities (including eye movement desensitization and reprocessing [EMDR], many somatic trauma therapies, and the polyvagal theory) are built on a foundation of the triune brain. This makes sense if their creators studied the triune brain model in college and were graded on their knowledge of it.

The continuing presence of this incorrect model is understandable, though unfortunate.

Tracking the lizard in the modern day

Because the triune brain model has been around for so long, its disconfirmed ideas have taken on a life of their own. If you hear people talking about their lizard brains or emotional brains, or that they're "acting from their amygdala," or that they need to "regulate their nervous system," they're calling back to the triune brain model.

The triune brain concept spoke deeply to people in Paul MacLean's day, and because of the research lag, it still speaks to people today.

How—and why—research lags persist

In part 1 of this article, I explored three reasons for the lags that restrict our access to high-quality, current research:

  1. Research is an elite occupation that is not open to everyone.
  2. The lengthy research lag further separates clinicians and the public from the elite world of research.
  3. There is built-in, unequal access to research studies, research communities, and their findings.

There is yet another reason, and it's a research norm that even some science journalists don't understand: Research is a verb. It's an activity, and it's a highly social one, where publication is not the final word, at all. Publication is often an invitation to argumentation with one's peers.

The science isn't decided on publication; it's communally built in responses, challenges, and conversations (some of which go on for years until confirmation is achieved).

As a result, you may be able to read a research study, but if you're not a part of its elite community of researchers, you may not understand the social context in which the study was created—and you may rush to judgment, or miss essential information that only insiders have.

I see this rush to judgment regularly in science journalism ("Eggs are healthy!" "No, eggs will kill you!" "No, egg whites are OK!"), and the confusion this poor reporting has created has made many members of the public—understandably—distrust research and science as a whole.

article continues after advertisement

The implications are weighty

The research lag and the inaccessibility of research have meant that we in the public don't receive the best information in a timely manner. This means that the forms of medicine, neuroscience, and psychology you and I can access are focused—in many cases—on outdated ideas and incorrect data.

Even if our clinicians have good intentions and the best information they can find, each of us might be relying on ideas that are decades out of date. For those of us focused on the social and emotional well-being of others, the ethical and professional implications of this situation are sobering.

Here are a few ideas to help us work around these structural obstacles:

Seek out subject matter experts who are actively connected to research

Popular books on science and psychological healing are selling you a viewpoint, and they're often more PR than they are grounded knowledge.

Instead, seek out people who are directly involved in research. Three of my go-to people are

  1. Psychological researcher Lisa Feldman Barrett's groundbreaking work on emotions and the brain have changed the face of psychology and neurology.
  2. Neuroscience researcher Birthe Macdonald has online courses that help therapists and counselors read research studies and find up-to-date information about therapeutic models.
  3. The hilariously brilliant science writer Mary Roach enters into numerous scientific communities to find the newest and strangest information on many fascinating subjects. She invites us into the highly social—and entertaining—world of research.
article continues after advertisement

And hold ideas lightly

The elite researchers I've known are not ideologues or self-promoters. They hold their ideas lightly enough to be able to invite critiques, and even to watch their theories get disconfirmed. Each of us should do the same, because if research communities are working as they should, all concepts and approaches may require updates or replacement. That's how the search for knowledge works.
